eds.name: King James Version
eds.note: The 66-book Protestant canon. Words in square brackets were supplied by the translators (printed in italics in the 1611 edition).

eds.name: World English Bible
eds.note: A modern public-domain revision of the American Standard Version (1901), with the 66-book Protestant canon.

eds.name: King James Version with Apocrypha
books: Song of the Three Holy Children
eds.note: As printed in 1611: the Apocrypha between the Testaments. The Church of England’s Articles (VI) say they are read “for example of life and instruction of manners” but not to establish doctrine.

eds.name: Douay–Rheims Bible (Challoner)
eds.note: The 73-book Catholic canon, translated from the Latin Vulgate. Esther and Daniel include the Greek additions; Baruch 6 is the Letter of Jeremiah. Psalms follow the Greek and Latin numbering (one lower than the Hebrew for most of the book).

eds.name: World English Bible, Catholic canon
eds.note: The 73-book Catholic canon in modern English, in Catholic order: Tobit, Judith and Maccabees with the historical books, Wisdom and Sirach with the wisdom books, Baruch after Lamentations.

eds.name: Septuagint (Brenton) with KJV New Testament
eds.note: The Old Testament of the Orthodox Church is the Greek Septuagint. Brenton’s 1851 translation includes the books Orthodox call anagignoskomena (“readable”): 1 Esdras, Tobit, Judith, 1–3 Maccabees, Prayer of Manasseh, Wisdom, Sirach, Baruch, the Letter of Jeremiah, Susanna, Bel and the Dragon and Psalm 151 (at the end of Psalms), with 4 Maccabees as an appendix. Psalm numbering is Greek. Brenton has no New Testament, so the KJV New Testament is paired with it.

eds.name: World English Bible, Orthodox canon
eds.note: The wider Orthodox canon in modern English, in Septuagint order, with Psalm 151, the Prayer of Manasseh and 3 Maccabees, and 4 Maccabees as an appendix. The Letter of Jeremiah is Baruch 6. The Old Testament text follows the Hebrew-based WEB for books shared with Protestants.

eds.name: Septuagint and New Testament in Greek
eds.year: Septuagint (Brenton’s Greek text); NT: NA28 text
eds.note: The Bible of the Greek-speaking Church: the Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Hebrew scriptures made from the third century BC and quoted throughout the New Testament, with the New Testament in its original Greek. Ezra and Nehemiah form one book (2 Esdras); Psalm numbering is Greek.

eds.name: Vulgata Clementina (Latin Vulgate)
eds.note: The Latin Bible of the Western Church for over a thousand years. Jerome translated most of it around 382–405; the Clementine edition of 1592 was the official Catholic text until 1979. The Douay–Rheims is its English translation, so the two can be compared verse by verse. Psalm numbering is Greek and Latin.
